Priors that make a cogmod posterior proper

Source: R/cogmod_priors.R
cogmod_priors.Rd

Fills in weakly informative priors for the parameters brms would otherwise leave flat, or give a default meant for another parameterization, for the model you are actually fitting.

For the families with a non-decision time this is not a convenience. brms gives the intercept of a custom-family parameter it does not recognise a flat, improper prior, and on the ndt + poutlier mixture the likelihood is exactly flat in two directions: poutlier toward 1, where every response belongs to the outlier component and the decision parameters drop out of the density, and ndt toward 0, where the gradient with respect to log(ndt) vanishes. Flat prior plus infinite flat region is an improper posterior, and the fit does not fail loudly: it returns intercepts around 1e14 with Rhat near 2 and an effective sample size of about 5. Several families have flat directions of their own (see Why these parameters).

Usage

cogmod_priors(formula, data, ..., warmstart = NULL, prior_scale = 3)

Arguments

formula

The model formula, as passed to brms::brm(). Must carry the family, i.e. be built with brms::bf(..., family = cogmod_lognormal()).

data

The data, as passed to brms::brm().

...

Passed to brms::get_prior() and brms::validate_prior(), for arguments such as data2 or knots.

warmstart

Optional. A previous fit to centre the priors on: a brmsfit, a cogmod_warmstart object, its data frame, or the path to a CSV of it, as cogmod_warmstart() takes. NULL (the default) leaves the priors where this function put them. Changes the posterior - see Centring the priors on a previous fit.

prior_scale

The prior SD, as a multiple of the source's posterior SD. Only used with warmstart. Larger is weaker; 1 would use the source's posterior as the prior.

Value

A brmsprior object, to pass to brms::brm(prior = ).

Details

The function starts from brms::get_prior() for the model in hand, edits the rows it has a better prior for, and returns the result of brms::validate_prior(): a brmsprior object, printed as a table that includes the defaults brms will use. Because every row comes from the model brms will build, no prior can miss its parameter - 0 + Intercept, interactions, group-level terms and smooths need no special handling - and a malformed specification errors here rather than inside brm().

Setting your own priors

Combine the result with brms::prior() entries. replace = TRUE replaces one of these defaults; without it the entry is added for another slot:

priors <- c(
  cogmod_priors(f, df),
  brms::prior(normal(-2, 0.1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "ndt"),
  replace = TRUE
)

Supported families

The family is read off formula, so build it with brms::bf(..., family = cogmod_lognormal()). Covered: every family with an ndt + poutlier component - cogmod_lognormal(), cogmod_logstudent(), cogmod_loggamma(), cogmod_invgaussian(), cogmod_exwald(), cogmod_bisa(), cogmod_gamma(), cogmod_invgamma(), cogmod_weibull(), cogmod_invweibull(), cogmod_logweibull(), cogmod_lba1() and the choice-and-RT families cogmod_lnr(), cogmod_rdm(), cogmod_lba2() and cogmod_ddm() - plus cogmod_exgaussian(), cogmod_geg() and the rating-scale families cogmod_choco(), cogmod_betagate() and cogmod_betadiscrete(). Any other family, or a formula carrying none, gets a message and brms's defaults unchanged, so the call is safe to leave in a script.

What gets set

For each parameter in the table under The priors:

  • its intercept gets the prior in the table;

  • its slopes get normal(0, 0.2) on the link scale, or the wider prior in the table. On a log or logit link a flat slope prior is not harmless: it can carry a condition into the flat regions while the intercept stays well behaved;

  • its group-level SDs get exponential(1), for the same reason, and the correlations keep brms's LKJ;

  • its smooth terms follow Smooth terms, as every smooth does.

Parameters not in the table, such as cogmod_lognormal()'s sigma, keep brms's defaults, and so does the response's own mu: its slopes are the effects being estimated, and brms's student_t() default is a fair intercept prior on most links. Two exceptions. cogmod_exgaussian() and cogmod_geg() give mu an intercept prior, because there it is a time in seconds on an identity link. And in the race families, cogmod_lnr(), cogmod_rdm() and cogmod_lba2(), mu is the rate of one accumulator, so its group-level SD gets the exponential(1) the other accumulator's gets and swapping the dec() coding does not change what the priors say.

A row brms left flat is filled. A row brms already filled is replaced only where its default was written for a parameter of the same name in one of its own families, and is wrong here: uniform(0, min_Y) on an ndt left out of bf(), the min-RT bound the outlier component exists to remove; gamma(0.01, 0.01) on cogmod_loggamma()'s shape, which must be free to go negative; and student_t(3, 0, 2.5) and the like on the sigma of cogmod_exgaussian() and cogmod_geg(), the shape of cogmod_geg() and the phi of cogmod_betagate() and cogmod_betadiscrete() - a Gaussian SD wider than most whole RT distributions, or on cogmod_betadiscrete()'s log link a precision reaching 2853.

ndt and poutlier

ndt is in seconds, like everything else in these families. normal(-1.2, 0.5) on its log link centres it on 0.30 s with 95% of the mass between 0.11 and 0.80 s: wide enough for slow populations and demanding responses, and still a fence against ndt -> 0.

poutlier is a proportion. normal(-6, 1) on its logit link centres it on 0.25%, with 95% between 0.035% and 1.7%, which is where the empirical estimates sit: Miller (2024) puts the outlier proportion below 0.5% across four lexical-decision megastudies, and the untrimmed data of the outliers article agree. If the data were trimmed before fitting, tighten the prior (normal(-7, 0.5)) rather than fixing poutlier = 0, which brings the hard min-RT boundary back; see the Trimmed data section of cogmod_lognormal().

On the link scale for a parameter in bf() - for its intercept, or under 0 + Intercept its coefficient named Intercept - and on the natural scale for one left out (see Parameters left out of the formula).

Parameters left out of the formula

Writing ndt ~ 1 and leaving ndt out are not the same model to brms. A parameter in bf(), even as ~ 1, gets a linear predictor and lives on its link scale, reported as ndt_Intercept under Regression Coefficients. One left out is declared as a plain auxiliary parameter, like sigma in gaussian(), and lives on its natural scale, under Further Distributional Parameters, so it needs a prior on that scale. The two columns of the table describe the same belief wherever they can: exactly on a log or identity link, where lognormal is normal on the log scale, and matched on the median elsewhere.

The exception is a probability whose omission is itself a statement. Leaving poutlier out says the data were trimmed or are not expected to contain outliers, and leaving pmid or pzero out says the event is not expected. Those get an exponential, with its mode at zero, which no logit-scale prior can have, and the same median: exponential(280) against plogis(-6) = 0.0025, and exponential(9) against plogis(-2.5) = 0.076. It is still a prior, so a genuine spike of fast responses still pulls the rate up.

Why these parameters

Each family's own page has the full account. In short, a parameter is in the table for one of five reasons:

  • Its link puts a limit at infinity, and the likelihood is flat long before it - the ndt -> 0 failure again. That is the start-point ranges (sigmabias) and the LBA and RDM thresholds that share a ridge with them (boundary), the between-trial variabilities (sigmadrift, sigmandt), and cogmod_logstudent()'s dof, which reaches the LogNormal only as dof -> Inf. Where the design cannot identify a range or a variability, fixing it in bf() (sigmabias = 0) is better than estimating it behind a prior.

  • An accumulator that stops winning. Push a race accumulator's rate down far enough and the likelihood stops depending on it, or on its SD: nuone and the SDs in cogmod_lnr(), driftone in cogmod_rdm() and cogmod_lba2(). Under dec(Error) that is the error accumulator, and wherever errors are rare its posterior sits in the lower tail of the prior: the fence working, not a prior at odds with the data. mu has the mirror plateau; if the rarely chosen option is on mu, copy the prior onto it.

  • An arbitrary scale. cogmod_lba2()'s likelihood is exactly constant along a ray that rescales every evidence parameter. The priors on sigmazero and sigmaone make the posterior proper; only fixing one of them in bf() (sigmazero = 1) identifies the scale.

  • A ridge with another parameter: tau with ndt in cogmod_exwald(), shape with mu in cogmod_geg(), dof with poutlier at the fast end of cogmod_logstudent(); and cogmod_loggamma()'s shape, whose prior also keeps the sampler clear of sigma * shape >= 1, where the density is unbounded at the shift.

  • Identified, but brms leaves it flat or gives it a default for another parameterization: the Wald and DDM thresholds, the DDM's bias, and the ex-Gaussian and rating-scale parameters (below).

No prior is set on the shape of cogmod_weibull() or cogmod_gamma(), although a shape below 2 makes their ndt gradient unbounded: the likelihood itself prefers that region, by around 100 log units on the data in the RT models article, so a prior weak enough to be a default could only bias it. ?rcogmod_weibull sets out what to do instead.

The ex-Gaussian and the GEG

cogmod_exgaussian() has no ndt, but mu, sigma and tau are all lengths of time in seconds, which brms cannot know. On the softplus link, sigma (the Gaussian SD) gets 25 to 330 ms with a median of 96 ms, and tau (the mean of the exponential tail) 55 to 630 ms with a median of 201 ms: the range they occupy across the usual simple- and choice-RT tasks. mu is on an identity link, where brms's default, a student_t() with a scale of 2.5 s, spreads the Gaussian's centre over several seconds either way, and under 0 + Intercept it gets no prior at all. normal(0.4, 0.25) puts 95% of it between -0.09 and 0.89 s and deliberately allows negative values: for fast, heavily tailed data the Gaussian component belongs near or below zero, with tau carrying the mass. It is the centre of the Gaussian alone, so the mean of the distribution is mu + tau. cogmod_geg() takes the same rows, and a shape centred on the ex-Gaussian it nests (shape = 1, with 95% between 0.37 and 2.7): shape and mu sit on a ridge, and the prior holds it.

The rating-scale families

cogmod_choco(), cogmod_betagate() and cogmod_betadiscrete() have no infinite flat region of the RT kind, but every parameter arrives either flat or with a brms default meant for another parameterization.

  • Point masses. pmid is the probability of exactly the midpoint, and pzero of an extra category outside the scale. When the event is absent from the data the likelihood rises all the way to zero, and under a flat prior the logit runs off to minus infinity: poutlier's failure, and poutlier's treatment. normal(-2.5, 1) centres it on 8%, with 95% below 37%. To switch one off, fix it in bf() (pmid = 0); a response exactly on the midpoint is then impossible, and the fit will not start.

  • Extremes. pex, the total probability of a 0 or a 1, is not given a mode at zero: extreme responding is a response style, not a contaminant. normal(-2, 1) centres it on 12%, with 95% between 2% and 49%. bex, which end the extremes favour, is centred on symmetric, which also keeps it away from 0 and 1, where one gate closes and every response at that end has zero probability.

  • Beta shapes. confright and confleft, the Beta means of each side, are centred on the middle of their half. The precisions are the awkward ones: below about 1 the Beta is U-shaped and unbounded at both ends, and a large one concentrates it sharply. normal(2, 1.5) on the softplus link spans 0.33 to 4.95, leaving 17% of its mass below 1, since a polarising item really can produce a U. cogmod_betadiscrete()'s phi is on a log link: normal(0.7, 0.8), 0.42 to 9.7 with a median of 2.

mu is left to brms, whose student_t(3, 0, 2.5) is the standard choice on a logit link.

Smooth terms

A smooth's SD, sds, is not in link units. brms writes the penalised part of an s() or t2() term as sds * Zs %*% zs with zs ~ N(0, 1), and how far one unit of sds moves the linear predictor depends on the basis mgcv builds: about 0.45 link units for s(x), 6 for s(x, bs = "cr") and 0.1 for t2(x, z, k = c(5, 5), bs = c("cr", "cr")), almost regardless of the data. So each smooth term gets exponential(rate), with the rate set to that term's own scale (read off brms::make_standata()): exponential(1) on the wiggle measured in link units, median 0.69 and 95% below 3, whatever the basis. A term whose scale cannot be computed gets exponential(1). This applies to every smooth, the response's included, and it matters however many rows there are: a smooth's SD is informed by the handful of coefficients behind each penalty, as a group-level SD is by the number of groups.

The unpenalised part of a smooth - the linear trend of an s(x), the marginal trends of a t2() - is reported under class b, where it would take its parameter's slope prior; but mgcv sets the scale of those columns, not the user. On the parameters in the table, each such column gets normal(0, s / rms) instead, which is the slope prior normal(0, s) stated on the trend at a typical row, rms being the column's root mean square.

Centring the priors on a previous fit

warmstart takes what cogmod_warmstart() takes - a brmsfit, the table as.data.frame() makes of one, or the path to a CSV of it - and replaces each prior with normal(median, prior_scale * sd), from that fit's posterior for the same parameter. It applies to the population-level intercepts and coefficients, the group-level SDs and the parameters left out of the formula; correlations keep their LKJ. A parameter the source never saw keeps the prior it would get anyway, and cogmod_warmstart()'s print() says how many there are.

This changes the posterior. Unlike cogmod_inv_metric() and cogmod_step_size(), which only change how the sampler moves, a prior is part of the model. If the source was fitted to data the new model also contains, it counts those data twice: a pilot on 5 of 10 participants used to centre the priors for all 10 uses those 5 twice, and the intervals come out too narrow by an amount nothing in the output shows. Use it when the source is an independent data set - last year's sample, another lab's, another session - or for a deliberately sequential analysis.

prior_scale = 1 makes the source's posterior the prior. The default of 3 has nine times its variance: enough to keep the sampler in the right region and out of the flat directions, weak enough for data that disagree to win.

# last year's sample as the prior for this year's
priors <- cogmod_priors(f, df, warmstart = fit_2025)
priors <- cogmod_priors(f, df, warmstart = fit_2025, prior_scale = 6)  # weaker

References

  • Miller, J. (2024). Estimating the proportions and latencies of reaction time outliers: A pooling method and case study of lexical decision tasks. Behavior Research Methods, 56(7), 7280-7306. doi:10.3758/s13428-024-02419-y

See also

cogmod_inits(), cogmod_stanvars(), cogmod_warmstart()

Examples

d <- data.frame(RT = rcogmod_lognormal(50, ndt = 0.3, poutlier = 0.02))
f <- brms::bf(RT ~ 1, sigma ~ 1, ndt ~ 1, poutlier ~ 1,
  family = cogmod_lognormal()
)
cogmod_priors(f, d)
#>                   prior     class coef group resp     dpar nlpar lb ub tag
#>  student_t(3, 0.8, 2.5) Intercept                                         
#>       normal(-1.2, 0.5) Intercept                      ndt                
#>           normal(-6, 1) Intercept                 poutlier                
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept                    sigma                
#>  lognormal(-0.35, 0.75) sigmabias                                 0       
#>   source
#>  default
#>  default
#>  default
#>  default
#>  default

# Replace a default, or append a prior for another parameter.
priors <- c(
  cogmod_priors(f, d),
  brms::prior(normal(-2, 0.1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "ndt"),
  replace = TRUE
)
